Madam Speaker, this bill arises out of the fact that when a young person, for example, receives an absolute discharge from a court he finds out sometimes three, four, or five years later when he seeks employment that he still has a criminal record.
The object of the absolute discharge and indeed the conditional discharge as produced in the Criminal Code was to make sure that young people in particular and people who receive absolute and conditional discharges do not have a criminal record.
Under the current circumstances they have, and that criminal record can only be removed by an application to the National Parole Board. That is a travesty and this act attempts to clean up that matter in law.

speechtext:
Atomic Energy of Canada Limited reports as follows:
(a) (i) (iii)
Each nuclear facility owner is required to submit a decommissioning plan to the Atomic Energy Control Board. The selection of a decommissioning method and the costs thereof are the responsibility of the nuclear facility owner. Substantial reactor decommissioning experience exists today. Since 1960, some 65 research, test and demonstration reactors world-wide have been decommissioned.
For the prototype nuclear facilities decommissioned by AECL, a method of long term isolated, secured storage for the reactor system has been used. All active process materials are removed from the system and then the reactor containment building is sealed and secured for a period of about 50 years. During this period, radioactive decay will very substantially reduce the radiation fields present when final decommissioning is subsequently carried out, making the work easier and safer. Most of the nuclear facility area outside of the reactor contain-

June 12, 1990
Government Orders
ment building can be cleaned and reused immediately. This includes the administration buildings, most of the service area and the turbine hall. Based on experience, through the decommissioning of the Nuclear Power Demonstration (NPD) reactor in Ontario, and the Douglas Point (Ontario) and Gentilly (Quebec) prototype power reactors, typical costs for this method would be expected to be about $30M (1990) for a commercial power reactor. The cost of final decommissioning after the 50 year radioactive decay period is estimated at $60M (1990). Potentially, the site would then be used for a new nuclear facility.
It is expected that the utilities would follow this practice. The utilities are already charging a small amount in the power bills, which is being accumulated with interest, to cover the cost of decommissioning. This amounts to 1 percent or less of the price of electrical energy produced.
(b) (i)-(iv)
In 1981, the governments of Canada and Ontario announced the review process for the concept of deep geological disposal of nuclear fuel waste. The process provides for regulatory and public hearings before site selection for a disposal facility begins. The governments stated that no site selection would proceed until after the concept had been approved. However, conceptual design studies related to site selection and the construction and operation of a disposal vault are being addressed. These are conceptual in nature and deal with reference situations with respect to both schedule and cost. No firm schedule or costs exist at this time. Accurate estimates can only be given when a specific site is selected and an actual vault designed.
Although no nation has yet disposed of its used fuel permanently, there is considerable experience in a number of areas related to disposal, e.g. mining, immobilization, packaging, transportation. Costs of a reference disposal vault including design, construction, commissioning, operation, transportation, decommissioning, and other activities have been estimated. Ontario Hydro has estimated that disposal of all used fuel from Pickering, Bruce, Darlington, and a future Darlington-type station could be carried out at a cost of $8.5 billion (1988 dollars), expended over a period of 80 years. These costs are estimated to be 5.1 percent of the levelized unit
electrical energy cost (LUEC), of a future Darlington-type station.
This estimate is consistent with cost estimates of International Atomic Energy Agency member countries, whose estimates range from 2 to 10 percent of electricity production costs. The Ontario Nuclear Cost Enquiry has noted that there is no practical way of checking the validity of Ontario Hydro's cost estimates at this time. Nevertheless, the Enquiry points out that, although the expenditures will be high when they are incurred, they comprise a very small portion of the levelized unit electrical cost, because of the long time-frame involved.
Canadian nuclear utilities include a charge in customer billing to cover future costs of nuclear fuel waste disposal.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to express the government's support for Bill C-52, which the Finance Committee reported to this House on the 7th of this month.
Bill C-52 constitutes a revision of the regulations governing retirement savings providing entitlement to a tax advantage, such as registered pension plans, deferred profit sharing plans and registered retirement savings plans. By setting out the objectives of tax advantages more clearly, this reform makes it possible for Canadians to accumulate a reasonable income for their retirement years.
With your permission, Madam Speaker, I would like to point out that the proposed measures are added to other reforms carried out previously to meet the need to promote retirement income security for our population. This, in a nutshell, is the proposal: Improvements in the benefits payable under the Canada Pension Plan and the spouse's allowance program; amendments to the contribution rates to guarantee the funding of the Canada Pension Plan; major improvements in the minimum contribution standards governing private pension plans, including particularly a shortening of the benefit purchase period and an improvement of the benefits to be paid to the surviving spouse.
This reform of the tax regulations is important because the present ceilings on tax assistance for retirement savings are not structured so as to help Canadians provide for an adequate retirement income. They vary widely depending on one's employment status; there is hardly any possibility of compensating for the loss of savings during past years; and, finally, it allows certain taxpayers to obtain excessive tax benefits by using various tax planning techniques.
The measures proposed in Bill C-52 deal with these problems directly. They provide for a standard ceiling equal to 18 percent of earnings, up to a maximum number of dollars. This uniform ceiling applies to all types of retirement savings with a tax benefit, whatever the plan or combination of plans.
Government Orders
They make it possible for taxpayers to use RRSP contributions to complement the savings they build up in employer-sponsored retirement plans-again up to the 18 percent ceiling. This uniform ceiling is therefore accessible to all Canadians, whatever their employment status.
By making it possible to carry unused RRSP contributions over for 7 years, they give Canadians a better chance to compensate for losses of savings sustained in previous years.
Finally, they are more equitable and provide for better cost control because they eliminate a number of tax planning mechanisms which allowed high income individuals to obtain excessive tax benefits.
The members of the Finance Committee have thoroughly studied the measures proposed in Bill C-52. They also heard a large number of witnesses and held consultations with labour organisation representatives and pension plan specialists. Following this consultation process, the Committee suggested a number of major changes in both the Bill and the regulations. Those changes were meant to simplify some of the legislative measures and to give plan administrators more flexibility in improving benefits and in offering additional pension entitlements in the case of family related leave or early retirement due to plant closures.
On June 7 last, before this House, the Minister for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs expressed the government's commitment to amending the first draft of the Income Thx Regulations to make it possible to implement the changes recommended by the Finance Committee.
On behalf of the Minister for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs, I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the members of the Standing Committee on Finance for the diligent manner in which they conducted their detailed examination of a lengthy and complex piece of legislation.
You will undoubtedly allow me to point out, Madam Speaker, that the tax payers of the electoral riding of Trois-Rivieres are anxiously awaiting this Bill, which provides for a major improvement of pensions in Canada and for the best possible combination of different pension plans.

June 12, 1990
Government Orders
In closing, Madam Speaker, I would point out that the examination performed by the Finance Committee followed a lengthy period of development and consultation concerning these important measures to improve the security of Canadians' income.
I hope that the Members will see fit to adopt this Bill, which is necessary and important for all Canadians, as rapidly as possible.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak in favour of Bill C-52.1 must be very honest and say that it is not a perfect bill. There are many problems with trying to correct inequities within the pension field, but I feel that this bill will right some wrongs and therefore I can say, as the lead speaker for the Liberals, we will support the bill.
Bill C-52, as amended, is designed to correct the inequities of the existing tax system which treats retirement savings for people who are members of the defined benefit pension plan differently from those for members of, for instance, deferred profit-sharing plans, and differently again from the ordinary self-employed Canadian or the employee whose company does not offer a pension plan at all.
This bill will also eliminate excessive and unintended tax deferrals. There have been, over the past few years, some loopholes, so to speak, which have allowed some very high income earners to use the tax system to accumulate very lucrative forms of pension. We feel that these loopholes must be closed. This bill addresses these loopholes and will prevent any further abuse of the system, we hope.
The objective of the tax reform in Bill C-52 is to ensure, with reasonable limits, fair and consistent access to tax assistance for retirement savings to encourage increased private savings now to meet pension needs in the future. We all agree that the current system is in need of revision and has been for some time.
Bill C-52 and its proposed system, as originally introduced in the House of Commons, needed a great deal of study. At the finance committee, we heard numerous witnesses, gave the bill much thought, and come up with a very different bill which is being considered today. The bill has been amended. There is an agreement to draft
regulations that will implement all the suggestions that the finance committee has made. The finance committee and all parties worked together co-operatively to bring about perhaps the best bill possible at this time.
In the past, the system of pensions in place in the past was simple. The only tax reporting was for employee pension contributions, deferred profit-sharing pension contributions, and RRSP contributions. There were no carry forwards. If one did not use up to one's RRSP limit in one year, one lost it.
The present pension regime is very inequitable. All non-contributory defined benefit plans are treated equally, regardless of how generous benefits are, as are all contributory defined benefit plans. Therefore, employees with very poor pensions and employees with very rich pensions all were able to contribute $3,500 to RRSPs according to their income. However, an employee with a poor 1.25 per cent contributory plan with a 5 per cent contribution earning $35,000 was restricted to an RRSP contribution of $1,750.
The proposed legislation attempts to right this inequity. I have talked about some abuses of the present pension system and we have all heard terms such as "flip-flop", "double-dipping", "off-side plans", and "designated plans"-a host of loopholes that benefited very high income earning people. We have absolutely no objection to high income earners preparing for retirement with a very high pension, but we object to them having tax assistance to do so. All people have to be treated equally with regard to tax assistance up to a certain level. If one wishes to have a better pension plan, then one is free to invest one's money, but after tax.
Canadians with company pension plans and those without will be given more equal treatment when it comes to saving for retirement. About two out of every three private sector workers do not have corporate plans, or about six million people out of a total workforce of 14 million. Currently, people building pensions only through RRSPs do not get the same tax assistance as those with company plans. Bill C-52 enables those self-employed persons to have the same tax relief as those with employers to invest in pensions for them. This bill will equalize the treatment between these groups. That is the main purpose of Bill C-52.
June 12, 1990

There are two basic types of plans. The first, to which most pension plan members belong, is the defined benefit plan. A defined benefit plan means certain benefits are guaranteed upon retirement. There is a wide range of plans. A rich plan may guarantee upon reaching the age of retirement 60 per cent or 70 per cent of the average salary earned five years prior to retirement. A good defined benefit plan may have the pension fully indexed. Some have no indexation whatsoever. It all depends on the kind of plan. Basically, these plans give a guarantee of what one will get on retirement.
The other basic type of plan is a money purchase plan which has a defined level of contribution, but no fixed level of benefits. What one receives in the end depends on how well the investment of these funds has done. The legislation attempts to equalize all kinds of systems.
The current limits place many Canadians at a serious disadvantage in saving for retirement. This includes many of those who are dependent on RRSPs, a group which includes the self-employed and employees without pension coverage. We know that in Canada the small businessmen, self-employed people in small businesses, are the ones who create the largest number of jobs, especially in the last few years. It is the biggest growing sector in our economy.
It is extremely important that these average Canadians-and they are very average Canadians who are out there working very hard trying to earn a living-also have the opportunity to invest in a reasonable type of pension. In this case if you are self-employed, then it will Ire through RRSPs. You will also be able to benefit from a similar advantage upon retirement after 35 years.
It is especially important to make these changes to the pension system now while the baby boom generation ages and prepares for retirement. The present pension system with all its unfairness in retirement tax assistance is improved under Bill C-52.
In the next 40 years the percentage of Canadians over 65 will double to 30 per cent.
The new rules attempt to standardize by 1995 the amount of tax relief for retirement savings which a
Government Orders
person can receive from the government by contributing to a pension plan, a deferred profit- sharing plan or to an RRSP. The proposal would set a uniform limit of 18 per cent of earnings that are eligible for tax assisted retirement savings.
One of the reasons for the 18 per cent is that if you invest 18 per cent of your wages over a 35-year period, you will be guaranteed roughly a 70 per cent return, or 70 per cent of your best three to five years of earnings in those five years. That is why the 18 per cent is used and not 20 per cent as is presently in place.
Most members of company pension plans will be able to contribute more money to their RRSPs under these changes. This bill, say many tax experts, goes a long way to correcting the unfairness and inflexibility of the current 13-year old pension system.
If individuals do not make their maximum RRSP contribution in a given year they will be allowed to carry forward for seven years these unused amounts. This will allow them to contribute more than the prescribed RRSP limit in one year, if they have under-contributed in a previous year. But pension income cannot be rolled over into RRSPs.
Why is there a seven year carry forward? It has been observed by the Department of Finance over the years that high-income Canadians are regular users of RRSPs over the course of their careers. However, the average taxpayer tends to concentrate RRSP contributions over the last 15 working years, which are particularly good economic years.
The average family in its early work life will save to buy a home and have a family, all extremely harsh economic realities which all families face. As the family ages, the children grow up. When the last few years of employment are reached, one may be in a better economic position. Children may have left home, or be self-supporting. The family home will probably be paid for. Therefore there will be more income to dispose of and one is more able to invest in RRSPs. That is the beauty of the seven year carry forward.
It will allow one to save that RRSP room, if one cannot make it this year or next year because a house was purchased. Perhaps four years from now one will receive a bonus and wish to use it to catch up on RRSP contributions. This can be done, thereby safeguarding

June 12, 1990
Government Orders
one's retirement years. Even though this may not always be done each year, there is a catch-up time.
Those who use RRSPs exclusively will have this seven year carry forward. Those who have pension plans ranging from poor plans to good plans will have in effect close to working lifetime carry forward periods. This provides a very positive incentive to establish even poor pension plans.
You have heard of the factor nine, Madam Speaker. There is quite a bit of controversy over the factor nine. The factor nine is a factor used to establish the value of the pension adjustment, an amount that will be shown on a person's T-4 slip. That in itself is what will give the person with a pension plan the amount of RRSP room that will be available for them to invest on a yearly basis.
If one has a poor pension plan, then clearly one will be better off dramatically because of the seven year carry forward. If one has a maximum pension plan, then one will be worse off. Those with average pension plans these will be considerably better off.
There is a form of rough justice. It is not perfect, and we are very much aware of that. It is felt that people contributing to pension plans under the age of 45 may be far more penalized in that their pension contributions before the age of 45 are not worth as much as what this pension adjustment will be. However, we are also very much aware that younger people tend not to take advantage of the RRSPs. The seven year carry forward will offset some of these disadvantages.
Under the pension reform in Bill C-52 very definitely the winners will be self-employed Canadians who do not belong to any pension plan at all. The winners will also be those who belong to very poor pension plans. They will experience the largest increase in RRSP contribution limits. The average Canadian is very much the one considered by this legislation.
I would like to describe the new RRSP limits proposed under Bill C-52. If you are not a member of a pension plan, currently you can contribute $7,500, or a maximum of 20 per cent of earned income to a registered pension plan. In 1991 this dollar limit will rise to $11,500, or 18 per cent of the previous year's earned income. The limit will then rise by $1,000 a year until 1995, when the limit
will be $15,500 per year. After 1995, the limit will be indexed to inflation.
If the individual is a member of a contributory pension plan where both the employer and employee make contributions, you can currently put $3,500 minus your pension contribution into an RRSP. In 1991, you will be able to contribute up to 18 per cent of your earned income, or $11,500 minus this pension adjustment, or PA as it is called.
This pension adjustment will be a figure that is calculated for each individual by their employer. It will be put on their T-4 slip. The greater the benefits from the pension plan the larger will be the pension adjustment. This pension adjustment will also include a $1,000 tax free area so that people in a defined benefit plan will still be better off than those just investing in RRSPs.
If you are a member of a non-contributory pension plan where only the employer makes contributions, you are currently allowed to put up to $3,500 in an RRSP. In 1991, this limit will increase to $11,500, minus your pension adjustment.
If individuals do not make their maximum RRSP contribution in a given year, they will be allowed to carry forward for seven years these unused amounts. This will allow them to contribute more than the prescribed RRSP limit in one year if they under contribute in a previous year.
We know that pension reform has been long overdue. It has been put off for far too many years. I would like to point out some of the recommendations made by the parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform set up by the Liberal government in 1983 and chaired by my predecessor, the member for Sudbury, the Hon. Doug Frith, which made the following recommendations.
First, it was recommended that people without pension plans be put on the same tax footing as people with pensions plans regarding RRSP limits. This has been addressed in Bill C-52.
It was also suggested that the existing system of RRSP tax deductions be converted to a fairer system of tax credits. This has not been implemented by Bill C-52, although the finance committee did study the implica-
June 12, 1990

tions of it. There was no easy answer. I will address this particular point as I go on with my speech this morning.
Third, it was recommended that a homemaker's pension be established and funded through the Canada Pension Plan and Quebec Pension Plan. That issue has not been addressed by this bill.
Fourth, the government should establish a 25-year contribution rate schedule for the CPP. Again, that has not been addressed by this bill.
Fifth, all private and public pension benefits should be indexed to some extent. Again, that has not been considered in this bill.
Some of these recommendations are not within the scope of this bill. Some others we will be looking into as quickly as possible.
In 1984 the then Liberal government in its budget proposed the very limits that are being proposed today because it was felt that it was only fair to allow the average Canadian to invest in an RRSP to ensure a pension at retirement.
In 1985 the present government promised pension reform. After announcing in the May, 1985 budget a new 1986 RRSP limit of $7,500 with further planned increases in the maximum RRSP contribution limits to 1990, in October of 1986 the finance minister announced that these future increases in RRSP limits were being changed. He announced that the maximum RRSP contribution limits for subsequent years would be lowered from what he had announced in 1985.
In June of 1988 before these changes could take effect the Minister of Finance announced that there would be a freeze in the maximum RRSP contribution limit for 1988, after which the maximum limit would rise to $8,500 in 1989; $10,500 in 1990; and rising by $1,000 a year until a limit of $15,500 was reached in 1995.
In August, 1988 the finance minister announced that these planned increases in the maximum RRSP contribution limit from $7,500 to $8,500 for 1989, which were announced in June of 1988, would be cancelled until after the election. In December of 1989 the government introduced the current pension reform legislation.
I have said that we do support this bill. We have some very serious fears in some areas where we feel that the legislation is perhaps not the best. Perhaps it is an issue
Government Orders
of timing. The timing is wrong. We want to continue to support this bill. But we feel that the pension reform package and the goods and services tax, which will both take effect in 1991, will discourage consumer spending at a time when the economy is predicted to be slowing down. We wish that were not so. I would rather see the government withdraw the goods and services tax than withdraw Bill C-52.
Higher RRSP limits will encourage savings and discourage consumer spending. The GST will also discourage consumer spending and encourage saving. Both take effect at the same time.
This pension reform will benefit average and better off Canadians who are in a financial position to take advantage of RRSPs. Many social groups such as the National Council on Welfare and the Canadian Council on Social Development have stated that these tax savings for relatively well off Canadians are excessive.
In 1986, 61 per cent of individuals with incomes over $45,000 made RRSP contributions averaging $4,057, while only 28 per cent of tax filers with incomes between $1,500 and $30,000 made RRSP contributions, averaging $1,987. Clearly, the better off received the majority of the tax benefits from RRSPs. By "better off" I am talking about people who are just above being very poor. They make up the bulk of the taxpayers. They are the ones who help finance the social programs which help the poor. We must allow that group of people the right to save toward better retirement.
We must also consider the problems of the poor. We at the finance committee have suggested that we study the Canada Pension Plan within the next year. We think it is extremely important that we consider the position of poor people, but not to the exclusion of average Canadians.
Another problem in terms of the timing of this pension reform package is that at the same time the government is giving this RRSP tax break to average Canadians, it is also implementing the clawback of senior citizens' pensions, imposing the GST and cutting unemployment insurance for the unemployed. The net result is that the burden of deficit reduction is being shifted from the wealthy on to the backs of lower income Canadians and the unemployed. Those least able to pay are being forced to pay more.

June 12, 1990
Government Orders
That bothers me very much because we are really not fully indexing the old age pension. We are not fully indexing the family allowance benefits, we are clawing them back. At the same time we are recognizing that full indexation is needed with pension reform so that after 1995 the $15,500 limit will be fully indexed.
In actual fact this proposal reduces what low income Canadians can contribute to RRSPs. For example, a person currently earning $25,000 and not part of a company pension plan can now contribute up to 20 per cent of their income to an RRSP, or up to $5,000. Under the new rules this amount will be reduced to 18 per cent of income, or $4,500 in 1991, $500 less than before. So while someone earning upward of $35,000 will have RRSP contribution limits increased, low income Canadians will be able to contribute less to their RRSP than before this particular bill. That is the fact.
It is also a fact that low income Canadians find it very difficult to invest in RRSPs, especially when they start off in their careers. It is hoped that because of the seven-year carry forward they will be able to recoup some of this loss.
We realize it is not an absolute answer, but 18 per cent is very much on what a lifetime pension is based. Thus we must for the sake of all stick with this 18 per cent.
The tax proposal does not require the indexing of pension benefits for all private and public pension plans, as was recommended by the 1983 Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform.
Ninety-three per cent of all members of private sector pension plans have no indexation against inflation for their pension benefits. It would have been very nice had this bill been able to put in place that type of indexation, but I believe it is not within the scope of this bill.
RRSP tax deductions are an unfair way of distributing income because the tax benefit from a $1,000 RRSP contribution is larger for higher income individuals than for low income people. The fairer solution would have been to convert RRSP tax deductions into tax credits. Currently, the tax benefit from a $1,000 RRSP contribution provides a tax saving of $450 for a person earning $45,000. The same $1,000 RRSP contribution provides a
tax saving of only $264 for someone with an income of $15,000. High income people save more in taxes because their marginal tax rate is higher.
Because of this unfairness caused by the deductibility of RRSP contributions, the 1983 Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform recommended that these deductions be converted into tax credits. With a system of tax credits the tax benefit from the $1,000 RRSP contribution would be the same for all taxpayers regardless of income. This would be a far more progressive and fair way of distributing the tax benefits from RRSP contributions.
The finance committee studied the implications of tax credits versus tax deductions. Consider, for instance, if we were to give a 26 per cent or 29 per cent credit to individuals. This would clearly benefit low income taxpayers with little or no adverse consequences for high income earners. However, the Department of Finance has estimated that such a move could add $1 billion annually to the costs. As you know, Madam Speaker, these are times of very strict budget controls. It is not at this time something that the government was prepared to recommend, nor was the finance committee prepared to recommend that at this time.
The recommendation of the finance committee is that it be studied so that perhaps a graduated percentage can be used. It has to be done in an economical way so that it does not cost the government gobs of money to implement.
We have asked the Department of Finance for a report on the possibility of changing tax deductions for retirement savings into tax credits. Included in this study would be the possibility of having more than one rate of tax credit, such as what is currently used for charitable organizations.
Under stage one of tax reform most deductions were converted into credits, a move that was supported by Liberals and social groups as being an improvement for the tax system.
Our present finance minister declared then that converting deductions to credits is a key element in achieving a fairer income tax system because credits give the same tax savings to all.
June 12, 1990

I know that an answer can be found when it comes to RRSP contributions. It must be found as quickly as possible.
Another problem is that Canadians will have to rely on their employers to calculate correctly a completely new number called the pension adjustment which will determine just how much they can contribute to their RRSPs. They may not have that figure as quickly as they would like, especially in the first few years. I believe that if most employees consult with their employers, they can be given a rough estimate of the amount of RRSP room they will have.
If they miscalculate in some way and are not given the total amount they would be allowed to invest in RRSPs, then because of the seven year carry forward they will be able to catch up that amount the following year. That will ease the transition. It would be far more serious if it were as it is today. That is to say, if you do not use it, you lose it. If, because we are not as comfortable with the new system as we should be, the wrong information is given out, then all is not lost. The following year you will have an opportunity to recoup.
One of the recommendations of the 1983 Parliamentary Task Force on Pension Reform was homemaker pensions. This is a very serious problem in Canada. It is a problem that by and large affects women. Women sometimes do take breaks in their careers. They do stay home. By and large, they are the ones who stay home and raise their children. They are often the ones who end up, perhaps, looking after an elderly relative. As a result, when they reach their retirement years they may have very little retirement income. It is a serious problem. It is a problem today when we look at many of our seniors, especially senior women who live on very, very low incomes. It is a problem that must be addressed.
This legislation does not set up a homemakers pension. I believe that the Canada Pension Plan people should definitely look into the matter. What this legislation does is allow that carry forward. For instance, say you have worked for 10 years and you could have invested in RRSPs but did not because you were interested in buying a house, buying furniture, getting established and then you start your family and leave the workforce. You would be able to carry forward those seven years of that RRSP room which you had not used in the last seven years of your work life. If you do not
Government Orders
work for 10 years, then when you do go back to work you can have a substantial portion of that carry forward in order to invest in RRSPs when you do return to the workforce.
That in itself is very much an improvement over the status quo. I know that there are many women out there who will be pleased with this. Again, it certainly does not go far enough. I will be the first one to say it. I have no illusions.
We must as a government give serious consideration to implementing a homemakers pension so that these people who do provide a very essential service within the home, the family and the community have the chance to accumulate some kind of retirement income.
The other area that is not considered by this bill is retirement income for part-time workers. Again, these people who work part-time, sometimes for the better part of their lives, must also have a chance at a good pension plan. There has to be some answer for these people. This is not within the scope of the bill. I recognize that, but I hope that in future we can right that wrong also.
The government's proposed Bill C-52 really does not address the issue of portability of pensions. Again, that is an issue which has to be considered. Other than a few minor technical changes nothing in Bill C-52 improves the portability of pensions, that is the ability of individuals to transfer lump sums from one pension plan to another when they change employers.
The 1983 task force made several recommendations that would give employees the right to take their accumulated pension benefits with them when they move to a new job. That has not been addressed in this case.
During the course of the finance committee's hearings on the bill we heard much testimony about the complexity of Bill C-52. There is no doubt in my mind that this was and continues to be an extremely complex bill.
For example, in a brief to the committee from the Canadian Institute of Actuaries the following was stated: "The degree of complexity inherent in the proposed system introduces the following problems: the level of comprehension of the new system among retirement plan members may be quite low, particularly in the first

June 12, 1990
Government Orders
two or three years, thereby threatening the acceptability of the system by the public."
I am convinced the changes that have been made to Bill C-52 take into consideration a lot of that complexity. I think the bill has been simplified to a very large degree, and I think that is extremely important.
The finance committee's eighth report to the Blouse has tried to simplify the legislation to address most of these concerns. We as a Liberal Party want something in place, and that is why we are supporting this bill.
The eighth report has been tabled, so I do not want to go through the full report. I believe anyone who wishes to read it may do so and will realize that some of the suggestions in Bill C-52 have been totally removed, such as pension adjustment reversal. That would have included in the bill an extremely huge component of complexity. By removing these PARs from Bill C-52 I believe that we have by and large reduced the level of complexity of the bill.
This bill definitely will not satisfy everyone, but we felt that by removing some of the complexities of the bill we were making the legislation simpler. We are leaving a certain amount of rough justice in the bill, and I believe that it important.
It is important that we have a pension bill which is easier to understand and easier to administer. It is always extremely difficult when one adds reams of complexities. It becomes an accountant's dream come true but an administrator's nightmare. We want to keep that nightmare down as much as possible.
Let me end by saying that I sat on the finance committee dealing with this bill. The huge amount of co-operation among all parties made me believe in this parliamentary system. I believe the finance committee should often, and perhaps at all times, work in this co-operative manner for the good of Canadians.
I realize that this was an impossible task for the committee when we were dealing with the GST legislation, but it felt very good to be able to work as a group with this particular piece of legislation and to add as many changes as we felt were feasible, with the co-operation of all parties and with the finance officials.
We as a Liberal Party are aware that it is not a perfect bill, but it is better to have an imperfect bill than to carry on the way we have for the last number of years. It was absolutely essential that we curb all excesses and that we close those loopholes. The closing of those loopholes means that the changes this bill is bringing forward will in effect be revenue neutral.
It is important that we not impose harsher penalties on the economic system of this country and on deficit reduction. I am pleased to see that that is a part of it. Perhaps the timing of the bill is not right, but that is not the bill's fault. It may be the fault of other pieces of legislation before this House with which my party and I happen to disagree.
I will end by saying that we are supporting this bill.

Madam Speaker, this bill in front of us this afternoon in fact is a piece of legislation which is tremendously important to people in the millions right across the country. We are going to see marked changes occur in the system by which the tax system of this country assists people to put money aside for pension purposes in the future.
I have to say that I am disappointed a minister has not come from the government to present this bill and to answer some of the criticism put forward from different directions since the final version of the bill was reported back to the House last week. I think some of those questions deserve answers. The correct and responsible people to be putting those answers forward are in fact members of the ministry of this Conservative government. It is very unfortunate that they are not here to meet those responsibilities.
The finance committee which has looked carefully at this bill reported back some changes the government agreed to accept. They were the consequence of significant negotiation between the finance committee and the Department of Finance. As members of the finance committee, many of us are here to take part in this debate today, but it has to be said very clearly that many of the points we wish to see brought forward as a finance committee had to be moderated in the negotiation with the Department of Finance because of its strong views with respect to this legislation.
If indeed it had been the finance committee itself which had been drafting this piece of legislation, it would have been a different piece of legislation than that which is before the House at the moment. This again puts the onus on the ministers responsible to be here to defend
June 12, 1990

this legislation and its many important ramifications for those receiving pensions, those contributing to pensions, those contributing to RRSPs and so forth in the years ahead in Canada.
The NDP has three main criticisms with respect to Bill C-52. The first and most basic criticism is that back in the 1960s we started in Canada to put in place the Canada Pension Plan, a plan which would be organized as pension plans are in so many other countries in the world through the public governmental system of this country. This would permit people to contribute throughout their working lives. Regardless of where they worked, whether they worked for someone or were independent small business owners, they could contribute to that plan. If they moved from job to job they could still contribute. There would be no cost for moving from one place of employment to another. There would be no cost in deciding to open a small business for a period of time and then coming back into the workforce. The Canada Pension Plan was something which would give people a pension to which they could contribute under any circumstance and in which they could accumulate benefits on a consistent continuing basis from year to year regardless of their circumstances.
Instead of recognizing the significance of the Canada Pension Plan initiative in the 1960s as the basis on which to move forward, with this approach to pension reform the government decided instead to take the Registered Retirement Savings Plan deductions available to people in the tax system and mesh this tax break with the private pension plan system in the country: registered retirement plans which take the form of defined benefit plans, money purchase plans, and profit sharing plans. There would be an heroic attempt to mesh together these different systems.
Inevitably in the process there have been some serious problems, difficulties, and inequities created. Although the finance committee has tried to improve upon them, we have certainly not been able to come up with anything close to effective and comprehensive answers to the ridiculous complexities and inequities created by the RRSP system, which in many respects should be the tail of the much larger pension dog. Instead in this approach
Government Orders
we have the tail of the pension dog wagging the whole system. We have the RRSP system and the need to make some kind of fair access to it for people in different circumstances in respect of private pension plans. We have that goal shaping what happens to the broad pension plan system. In the process, we miss the fact that we had a basic Canada pension plan system that could and should have been expanded. Therefore it would have given a system of portability and indexing that responds to Canadians and which would have been straightforward, fair and the same for people regardless of whether they were in small businesses in good parts of the economy or in declining parts of the economy.
The Canada Pension Plan would have provided fairness and equity. Also, it would have given a level of retirement earnings to people across the country once they were outside the workforce. This would have provided security for them once they faced older age. That is not the approach which is taken.
The other thing an approach relying on the Canada Pension Plan would have done is what has happened in Quebec, for instance.

One can see in the province of Quebec that a public savings system has created a large fund to promote development within the province. The Quebec Deposit and Investment Fund, for example, is a product of the public pension plan.

This kind of approach, which would have given us funds created through pension plan creations and contributions, would have given us a basis for really promoting economic development fairly and effectively throughout the countiy. We have missed that, too, by the fact that this approach to pension plans and pension reform has not made the Canada Pension Plan the central part or central concern of pension reform.
Our second broad criticism is that Bill C-52 gives most of its benefits to relatively well-off Canadians. It does so by expanding the RRSP contribution limit from $7,500 a year to $15,500 per year for those outside a pension plan. It is true that this higher limit is phased in until 1995. In 1995, the projections are that it will be at a level of 2.5 times the average industrial wage, which is in fact a lower

June 12, 1990
Government Orders
level than was the case in the past for maximum RRSP contributions.
Nevertheless, it is a significant increase in benefits to those making between $40,000 and $80,000 per year. The cost of these improvements to those relatively well-off Canadians comes first from eliminating something with which we agree, a series of abuses by high income earners in our pension system. I will talk more about that later. I will talk more about that later, Madam Speaker.
Second, the cost of these improvements for better off Canadians also comes from a reduction in the amount of RRSP contribution which is possible for some existing pension plans in which there are high employer contributions and low employee contributions. For example, the telecommunications workers' union in British Columbia will see their members lose from $1,000 to $2,000 per year in potential contributions to RRSPs.
It does not make sense to see losses for lower income Canadians such as those in the telecommunications workers' union in B.C. coming at the expense of benefits going to those high income earners who are going to receive these extra benefits from the significant increase in RRSP limits. That cannot make sense if we are talking about improving equity in the pension reforms that are before this House.
Finally, the last crucial criticism we make of this legislation is that the rest of the income tax system now works on the basis of tax credits. Tax credits provide a benefit to those people who are low-income earners, which is just as important to them in dollar terms as the tax credit provides to higher income people. If you have deductions instead of tax credits, the consequence is that the person who benefits most is the person with the higher income who is in that higher tax bracket. Therefore, there is a bigger gain from the same amount of benefit because it is a deduction at a higher tax bracket.
Our party argued hard within the finance committee to move to a system of tax credits. This is what we have in the rest of the tax system now. It has been proved that it is not impossible to do. But in fact the Department of Finance was not prepared to give ground on this issue. They have agreed, and it is an important agreement which our finance committee has managed to achieve, to
investigate this and come back with a report to the finance committee to see if there is some way of putting tax credits into effect in the future in the pension system. But it is something that should have been done before this broad set of pension reforms came into effect rather than as an afterthought.
There are improvements which our work in the finance committee managed to achieve. As originally drafted, the bill reduced significantly the possibility of trade unions bargaining for improvements in company pension plans through new collective agreements. We fought for and won changes in the regulations so that unions will have much more scope to bargain for such improvements.
For instance, the original bill blocked early retirement options in the case of plant closures or automation. We fought for changes to this and we were successful. Women were hit in the original bill by limits on the period of broken service for child rearing which they could take advantage of. These limits have been extended from five to eight years and made more flexible. This is another victory about which we feel good.
The original bill had a strong bias against defined benefit pension plans, the kind that most unions work out with their employers. These biases have been changed by simplifying administrative procedures, by increasing the amount of RRSP contributions that members of these plans can make in a number of cases and by making the rules clearer for pension portability.
Finally, we won commitments from the Department of Finance to examine tax credits for use in the future and also to look at how it is possible to use RRSP contribution space in a way that limits it for higher income earners in the future. We also won commitments from the finance committee to review the system in operation in three years and to examine how the Canada Pension Plan itself could be expanded in the future.
There are problems that remain but the last point that we would want to stress, is that this bill does plug some very important loopholes by which upper-income individuals were taking massive advantage of the tax system. We put pension maximums in place for higher income earners. A person with a $86,000 income will be able to
June 12, 1990

get 70 per cent of that as a maximum pension. You will not be able to go up to massive levels as in the past.
The current practice for many senior executives was to give themselves maximum RRSP room until close to retirement, then create a pension plan into which they could make retroactive payments. That double dipping is blocked.
We have blocked a number of important loopholes but we still do not have the pension reform system which our party envisions. We should have started, but did not start, in this case, from the Canada Pension Plan and which would have given us a chance to give portability, a chance to give fairness and a chance to give openness to every employee throughout this country.
I hope in the future that that is what we achieve in pension reform.
