Madam Speaker, I have been listening to my colleague, and I found him very eloquent and most interesting when he discussed the reform of the retirement pension system in Canada. I am always interested in knowing, when he talks about tax credits vs. deductions-I know that the government is carrying out a study to see how it could perhaps do one or the other, how it can use tax credits to reform pensions, but I would like my colleague to explain why, in the past, the government has objected to use a system which appeared much more progressive, more sensible, a system which, I can say it here in the House of Commons, is rational. Why has it refused until now to resort to a tax credit system? Secondly, if the government had objections to using such a system, what were they?
Those are my two questions, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I agree with my colleague that it is difficult to understand why the government did not accept suggestions to have a credit system rather than a deduction system. But I think it may have had two reasons to do so. The first reply given by the government was that it was too complicated to grant credits rather than deductions. But I find that very difficult to believe, Madam Speaker,
Government Orders
because we already have credits throughout most of our income tax system.
We have credits for charitable donations, and we also have credits for such things as the expenses of children attending university. We can continue with this part of our income tax system.
If it is not too complex for this part of our income tax system, I do not think it can be said, then, that it is too complex for our retirement pension system.
The other objection raised by the Department of Finance, to the effect that it may cost more than at present, is in my view very difficult to understand, considering that the credit system can be organized in such a manner as to give the same result for income as for expenditures, just as we have now with the deduction system.
I really do not think that this reply is acceptable. The Bill would need to be amended considerably to establish a system of credits, but then it has already been amended considerably in other areas. I believe it is possible to do the same thing with regard to the credits.

speakeroldname: Mr. Howard Crosby (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to put a brief question to the member for Essex-Windsor.
In his presentation, he mentioned the practice of double-dipping. This concept has provided difficulties over the years. I suppose there are arguments that might be made in favour of double-dipping. If a person has legitimately earned a pension and after retirement can provide services that have a specified value, it is proper that they make a claim for those services.
The case that we often find is where two payments are being made from the same source, particularly when that source is public such as the Government of Canada, and a person is receiving both a pension and a salary or fee for services.
However, one could argue that the combination of past government services and a fee or salary from the private sector is all right. If it is all right in those circumstances, why should the government not take

June 12, 1990
Government Orders
advantage of services from persons who have already retired and are receiving a pension?
I would like to ask the member for a more definitive statement from his point of view. Is he in favour of two payments being made to one person from the same source, whether that source is government or a private concern? If he is not in favour, does he think legislation should be enacted to prevent it?

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the question. Frankly, one of the things which is a problem with pension legislation like Bill C-52, is that it has a special, complicated vocabulary all of its own. We spent hours in the finance committee talking about PAs and PARs and PSPAs and all sorts of other acronyms that I am sure left many people who were watching the committee completely confused. At times it left many of us as committee members completely confused.
Double-dipping, as used with reference to this bill and in discussing what the bill attempts, is a different issue than the one raised by the hon. member. The member has raised the question of whether somebody who has been appointed, for instance, to head the CBC or something like that, should be receiving a pension as, for example, for time spent as a member of Parliament. I could make some personal comments with respect to that. I cannot make a comment with respect to our party's position on it, so I would prefer to stick to the meaning which is dealt with in the bill itself.
In the bill itself, double-dipping refers to the practice whereby people make RRSP contributions to the fullest possible extent for the period of their working life. This tends to apply especially to the owners of corporations and businesses of various kinds. Having made those massive RRSP contributions which would not be possible if there had been a pension system in place in the operation previously, just before they are due to retire they create a pension system for the business. They make back payments which make it possible for them to receive, after they retire, both the complete benefits of a pension plan and the complete benefits of the largest possible RRSP contributions. They would not have been able to do that if the pension plan itself had actually been in effect all those years that they were making RRSP contributions.
This bill prevents that kind of back payment from taking place and therefore prevents double-dipping. It is in that sense that we very much support what is suggested in this bill.

Madam Speaker, I would like to commence my little talk here today with a quote that I would like to expand on as I go along.
This quote comes from the Hon. Stanley Knowles, the former member of Parliament for Winnipeg North Centre, who stated in the House of Commons on November 9, 1964:
What I like most of all about the Canada Pension Plan-about the two stage plan which we are now developing for Canadians in their years of retirement-is that we are trying to reach a position where we are providing pensions that are adequate-I do not suggest that the levels which will be achieved by combining the Canada Pension Plan, at its best, with old age security, at its present level, are really the last words in adequacy, but at least we are talking about pensions of quite a different order front that what seemed to be accepted a few years or decades ago. I hope that, having accepted the principle that retirement security should be on the basis of adequacy, we will go on improving that basis, finding means and ways of raising the levels of our pensions so that all Canadians can look forward to a retirement in decency and dignity.
I would suggest that what we have at present is a continuation of that thrust toward adequacy, decency, and dignity. I wonder whether in fact we are choosing the route that we should be taking when we look at the lower and middle income earners in Canada.
Personally, I have no objection to some form of registered retirement savings plan that all Canadians can benefit from by putting away some of their extra earnings now to be used at a future date. It ensures that they do not have to live in abject poverty and that they can live in some comfort in their older years.
However, I question the thrust we are going in. If this is pension reform that we have on the table before us, then I question the direction in which we are proceeding in that pension reform.
It seems to me and the New Democratic Party that we should be looking at more basic reforms that look at the adequacy of the Canada Pension Plan and reforms that look at ensuring that all Canadians, regardless of how much money they have in their younger years, can live at
June 12, 1990

least at the same level, or at a reasonable level, in their retirement years.
Can that be done through the present registered retirement savings plan? Certainly, if we look at the changes that are before us, we can see that in the present system those who have $7,500 in additional income at the end of any one year can put that money away for later years, tax-free for the time being. They can draw on that and pay the taxes perhaps at a lower income level. I do not have too many difficulties with the concept, but let us look at what we have in this bill.
The proposal is that in 1991 the registered retired savings limit will go up $4,000 to $11,500; in 1992 to $12,500, in 1993 to $13,500, in 1994 to $14,500, and finally in 1995 to $15,500. It is interesting to note that those who will be able to contribute the limit in 1995 of $15,500 are those who earn $83,111. How many people in Canada will be able to use that?
I would suggest that people with earnings in the $80,000 plus bracket have other means of investment, and can look after their retirement years without the necessity of looking at a program that allows them to defer even more taxation.
This brings me to another section of this bill, which drops the limit from 20 per cent to 18 per cent of earnings. Who does that drop help, or who does it hinder?
Dropping the earning limit to 18 per cent as the maximum which can be put in registered retirement savings plans again hits out at those in the lower and middle-income scales, those of us who make $30,000 or $40,000 and are able to take some of that money each year and invest it for our retirement. I would put an asterisk beside that because at some of those rates it is very difficult for a one-earner family to make a living, and support children and a spouse. However, if there was money left over at the end of that period time, if you were an excellent money manager and wanted to put in the maximum amount, we have seen the maximum amount eroded for those in the lower-income levels.
Where are we going with our legislation? Is this how we are going to look after the vast majority of people in Canada? I would suggest no, because perhaps 5 per cent of the people of Canada will benefit by the upper limits
Government Orders
by 1995 of $15,500. Where is the fairness? Where is the equity for average Canadians? It is not within this bill. There are definite problems, I believe, with dropping that limit. It strikes out at the 95 per cent of wage-earners in Canada who do not have an $83,100 income and the ability to use the maximum. As I stated, it is those in the upper limits who really do not require that additional amount of money.
There is now a deferral system within the new legislation which allows contributions to be carried forward for seven years. I have said this in the past and I would like to repeat it. On the surface, it appears this is and can be a provision that can be used reasonably by Canadians who, perhaps, one year through some particular problem within their own employment area have had an income drop and they have the ability to cany forward. However, once again for the most part, this is a provision that can be used most beneficially by those in the higher income brackets.
It is not hard to imagine a person in a higher income bracket finding an investment opportunity to invest part of the money he would normally put into a Registered Retirement Savings Plan. He invests that money because, for one reason or another, he can get a higher return on it than he can deferring his $15,500 in tax through the Registered Retirement Savings Plan and the following year or years he then takes the money, adds on, and receives the tax deferral. I would suggest that this will be of limited benefit to lower and middle-income Canadians.
I cannot emphasize strongly enough that to benefit the majority of Canadians, the thrust of pension reform must be through a proper reform of the Canada Pension Plan. Then all Canadians, regardless of the amount they earn during their working years, can live with some dignity and comfort, as was stated by Stanley Knowles in the House of Commons in 1964.
Would it not be nice to be able to have a Canada Pension Plan system in place that allowed all Canadians a reasonable income of one-half of their earnings throughout their lifetime. This is not beyond our grasp. If it is something that we as parliamentarians want and set as a priority, I would suggest that it is within our grasp, something that is attainable.

June 12, 1990
Government Orders
All Canadians deserve to be treated reasonably and fairly in their declining years. As the population curve for seniors goes up, we know that across Canada 11 per cent of our population are over 65 years of age. The projections show clearly that will be doubled within approximately 30 years.
From my own personal experience in the riding of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt, there are pockets of population within Canada where the seniors' population is sometimes triple the national average. People cluster together. People go to areas that are easier on them in their old age. As we go on into the next 30 years, these people need some assurances that there will be something to assist them in their declining years, not simply because they have had the good fortune to be high income earners-some of the 5 per cent-but because we as Canadians are willing to assist each other with our equalization payments.
We are proud Canadians. We are proud because we have through history assisted and helped each other. We have the start of a system that can be second to none, but we need the political will to proceed with that system and to do exactly what I have stated. Let us give seniors and our own generation some hope for the future, some hope for that dignity, some hope for that decency, some hope for that equality in the retirement years.
Let me move on to some of the other measures within the bill and some of the problems about which other people have spoken.
In a news release on June 8,1990, the Telecommunications Workers Union talked about the legislation and emphasized that the only people who will be helped are the higher income earners. Mr. Larry Armstrong, president of that union, stated in that release:
There is no good reason for this legislation. It will harm pensions plans. It will harm individual Canadians. It will make our prospects of adequately taking care of an increasingly older population much more bleak. The only clear beneficiary will be the government treasury.
He goes on to state:
Starting in 1991, if this bill passes, Michael Wilson knows that he no longer will have to give millions of Canadians as much tax relief for saving for pensions. This could well add up to billions of dollars of tax revenue for the government.
Mr. Armstrong tells us further that the minor changes recommended by the chair of the finance committee will not undo the terrible damage this legislation will create.
A recent article on the pension bill in the Financial Post stated that actuaries were opposed to the provisions which are before the House today. In the article it states that they:
-object to the committee's proposal to drop provisions known as pension adjustment reversals (PARs) to simplify the new rules.
The legislation reduces individual registered retirement savings plan limits if the worker is part of a corporate pension plan. The formula used to reduce the RRSP limit is called a pension adjustment (PA).
The article quotes pension consultants at William M. Mercer Ltd. as saying:
-the proposal means young people who switch jobs lose retirement savings opportunities. They said some measure must be adopted to reflect the age of a pension plan member.
The amendments proposed by the finance committee make matters worse. "If PARs, pension adjustment reversals, are dropped, pension adjustment must be adjusted by age. The amendment approach is a disaster", states vice-chairman, Robert Dowsett, of William M. Mercer Ltd.
Another Canadian Press release of June 8 states:
-one pension expert said last-minute amendments have turned the legislation into a disaster for younger workers who may change jobs several times during their careers.
The article quotes Mr. Mercer as stating that because the bill no longer lets people increase their RRSP contributions to make up for lost pension benefits when they change jobs that this particular section is a disaster.
It appears that there are many difficulties with this legislation. The difficulties are not simply in some of the things that the pension adjustment people have pointed out. I would suggest part of the problem is the complexity of the terms and conditions within the bill.
How do we, the average wage-earner in Canada, look at these bills and find out how they are going to affect pension plans that we have within our unions, within our companies or, for that matter, carry forward some of the provisions within the bill. How is the bill going to affect us, the average wage-earner?
June 12, 1990

I would suggest that many of us legislators do not fully understand all of the implications and provisions of this bill. In looking at what some of the experts have said, it is obvious they feel that this is a disastrous bill. The complexity is one of the things that has been criticized by tax experts and adjusters.
How are we, the average wage-earners, going to find out where we should go? We are going to have to pay out more of our hard earned income to go to tax experts to have them tell us how we can best use this bill, how we can invest for our future, instead of having a simple system of deductions for Canada Pension Plan.
That is the route we should be going in the future, a look and a review of the basic Canada Pension Plan so that all Canadians, regardless of income, can live their ancient and dying years in comfort.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member. After Question Period we shall proceed with a period of questions and comments relating to the speech.
It being one o'clock, I do now leave the chair until two o'clock this day.
At 1 p.m. the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Madam Speaker, a parliamentary tradition was fulfilled last night when the pages met the MPs on the ball diamond.
It was a hastily organized match that even required assistance from Hansard. We forgot the need for bats and balls, but Bob Allen from Hansard was there with what we needed.
The MPs spotted the pages an average of 25 to 30 years. It was a classic match of experience versus youth and enthusiasm. All three political parties were represented, and the outcome proved that when we in this House co-operate, play by the rules and work together, the outcome will be obvious.
The MPs broke tradition and easily defeated the pages. We won in more ways than on the field. We got to know a few of the pages better, and the more I know of these young Canadians the more impressed I am. They have served this House well during the past year, and they have proven to be a credit to themselves and to this country.
We owe them our gratitude. I thank them for then-sportsmanship, their patience, their sense of humour and for being young Canadians of whom we can all be proud.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister told Canadians that free trade would mean lower prices for consumers who would save $800 a year as tariffs were removed on manufactured products. Now, consumers are being told by the government that, with the GST, they can expect the cost of manufactured goods to drop 6.5 per cent.
I have a list of prices for manufactured goods such as washers, springs, flanges, saw blades and so on covering 1988-90 which shows the Canadian consumer was sold a bill of goods on free trade as prices have increased on an average of 5.2 per cent while tariffs have decreased by 2.3 per cent.
With free trade, consumers called for independent monitoring of prices to ensure the consumer benefit. The government said the market will take care of it. The market players did take care of themselves.
Now with the GST, the government is again ignoring consumers' calls for an independent monitoring to ensure savings between the MST and GST are passed on to consumers. Again, the government says the market will take care of it, meaning that the market players will take care of themselves.
It is time this government took care of the taxpayer, instead of taking care of only big business.

June 12, 1990

Madam Speaker, since this is National Access Awareness Week and also International Literacy Year, I would like to emphasize the importance of providing literacy training for people with functional disabilities.
In a rapidly changing world, where competition is becoming increasingly fierce, it is a foregone conclusion that education is more important than ever before.
A good education offers better employment opportunities. It opens the door to a whole new world of ideas, to new knowledge and skills that will help the individual realize his full potential.
However, for some disabled persons, access to education may be limited due to the very nature of a functional disability that makes it harder for them to learn to read and write.
Since this is International Literacy Year, Madam Speaker, I urge those who work with the disabled and are involved in teaching to join forces, in order to adapt literacy training to students with special needs and thus give them a chance to take full advantage of the opportunities that come their way.

speakeroldname: Mr. Vincent Della Noce (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last week, the three members from Laval-Guy Ricard, former member of the Laval executive, Jacques Tetreault, first mayor of Laval, and myself, a permanent resident of this beautiful city for 24 years, jointly tabled three bills aimed at changing the names of the ridings of Laval-des-Rapides, Laval and Duvernay.
Madam Speaker, today Laval, which consists of 15 former towns, celebrates its twenty-fifth birthday-25 years of love and friendship.
When I entered politics in 1984, Madam Speaker, believe it or not, the riding of Duvernay was designated as Montreal-Duvernay, which I had changed to Duvernay. I fail to see why the federal ridings still bear the names of former towns, and I am thinking of my own riding, Duvernay, which includes five of these lormer
municipalities: Auteuil, Vimont, Pont-Viau, Saint-Frangois, Saint-Vincent-de-Paul and Duvernay.
The new bills will substitute Laval East for Duvernay, Laval Centre for Laval-des-Rapides and Laval West for Laval.
These changes will make it easier for Laval residents to identify with their respective federal ridings.
Thank you, Madam Speaker, and happy birthday to all the people of Laval!

Madam Speaker, over one year after the Exxon Valdez violated the Alaskan ecosystem with 270,000 barrels of oil, Canadians are still waiting for the report of The Public Review Panel on Marine Spills. The panel, announced by the Prime Minister last June, is all the more important while Petro-Canada courts disaster on the Grand Banks off Newfoundland.
PetroCan is drilling a wildcat well, but is unable to drill a relief well to contain a blow-out. An oil spill 32 times greater than the Valdez could occur without necessary emergency response. The chances of a spill from the well may be remote, but that is what they said about the Alaska tanker route during its years of safe operation. Until last March.
In the event of a major chemical or oil spill in the Great Lakes or on either coast, the Coast Guard, Transport Canada, the Auditor General and even the interim report on spills say that the government is not ready.
I urge the government to finalize the marine spill report so Canadians know that all plans and policies are in place for a disaster in our waters.

Madam Speaker, in January, the government removed exemptions to radio licence fees for municipalities. The li-
June 12, 1990

cences cover radios used by emergency services such as ambulance, fire and police.
The new regulations which in effect downloads costs on to local governments have had an enormous impact in my riding. Municipalities from Saanich to Sidney are faced with increases of 400 to 1,400 per cent. This not only imposes an excessive tax on over-burdened municipal budgets, but clearly demonstrates this government's willingness to raise revenue at the expense of health and safety.
This creative bookkeeping may help the federal balance sheet, but it hardly meets the needs of taxpayers. Forcing another level of government to choose between public safety and reductions in other services may be the most cynical deficit-cutting move the Conservatives have attempted.
Once again, this government has failed to consult. It has failed to act in the interest of the people it is supposed to serve, and it has failed to admit an error and roll back the radio licence fees. On behalf of my constituents, I strongly protest this outrage.

Madam Speaker, The "City of Champions", Edmonton, the Hobbema Four Nations and Enoch, Alberta, will host the First North American Indigenous Games from June 30 to July 8. I invite all members of this House to attend these historic games and encourage all their constituents to do likewise.
The games will open with a traditional Ceremonial Run from Wyoming, after elders offer prayers in our spiritual ceremonies. Todd Buffalo and Dennis Samson's rodeo will follow at the Penee AgriPlex in Hobbema on June 20.
Welcome to all those 3,000 plus indigenous athletes from North America and elsewhere who will be competing in these Olympic-style games. Events include archery, basketball, shooting, wrestling, soccer, track and field, volleyball, canoeing, boxing, lacrosse, a marathon, swimming, softball and golf. Welcome also to those who
will be participating in the cultural events, which is the important centre of our way of life.
Thank you in advance to two brothers, Charles Wood and John Fletcher, the sponsors and the hundreds of volunteers who are making my dream come true. This is a good, positive contribution that will encourage indigenous youth all over to pursue excellence, whether it is physically, mentally, culturally or spiritually.

Madam Speaker, this government's high interest rate policy is crippling the housing industry in this country and killing the hopes of thousands seeking affordable housing.
Housing starts and sales are down 40 per cent from last year. Thousands of construction workers and thousands of workers in related industries are losing their jobs.
Housing is a very important contributor to the Canadian economy and to our social well-being. It represents $43 billion and 670,000 person years of employment; that is 5 per cent of the total employment in Canada.
Housing is more than bricks and mortar, it is about people, young families, seniors and the physically challenged. This government, instead of telling Canadians "don't worry, be happy", should immediately reduce interest rates, scrap the GST and recommit itself to housing Canadians, especially the homeless and those on waiting lists for social and co-op housing.
Housing is not only good economic policy, it is good social and family policy and it is good environmental policy.

subtopic: PARISHES OF ST. IGNATIUS LOYOLA, IN GIFFARD, AND ST. GREGORY'S, IN MONTMORENCY
PARISHES OF ST. IGNATIUS LOYOLA, IN GIFFARD, AND ST. GREGORY'S, IN MONTMORENCY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the life of every community, there are milestones that should be pointed out. This is the case for St. Ignatius of Loyola parish in Giffard, which is

June 12, 1990
5. 0. 31
proudly celebrating the 75th anniversary of its founding this week, and for St. Gregory's in Montmorency which throughout the year is celebrating its 100th anniversary.
Madam Speaker, I wish to pay tribute today to the builders of these two communities in the riding of Montmorency-Orleans who have laid the foundations for the economic and social development of their communities.
Now part of greater Beauport, these two formerly independent municipalities contribute actively to the development of Quebec's fourteenth largest city.
I want to thank the celebration organizers for their dedication. Thanks to them, the people of Giffard and Montmorency will have an opportunity to find in their past the values and examples that will help them ensure the future of their community and of the generations to come.

Madam Speaker, last week Statistics Canada informed Canadians that 165,000 jobs were lost in the manufacturing sector last year. The Tory government's disastrous policies have claimed another victim. This morning, it was announced that Fruehauf Canada, this country's largest trailer manufacturer, is closing its Brantford plant, resulting in a loss of 334 direct jobs and as many as 1,500 indirect jobs. It is quite clear that a trio of Tory policies are directly responsible for this closure: free trade, deregulation and high interest rates.
In 1988, United States freight companies hauled about 15 per cent of all freight in Canada. This year that will rise to 60 per cent. The result is that Canadian manufacturing jobs are being lost and Canadian industries are being killed off.
Quite clearly, the level playing field promised by the Mulroney government is anything but level. Equally as clear is the fact that the government's free trade deal, its blind drive to deregulate and its policy of squeezing out Canadian jobs with high interest rates are killing the Canadian manufacturing sector.

Madam Speaker, I was very surprised to learn that the leader of the Parti Quebecois in the National Assembly, Jacques Parizeau, prefers appointing senators to electing them. It is especially surprising given the opinion of former Quebec Premier Rene Levesque that the Senate should be abolished.
For many years, at least twenty, Madam Speaker, Quebecers like Canadians from coast to coast believed that the Senate needed to be thoroughly reformed, not totally abolished.
Therefore the arguments the leader of the Parti Quebecois is making in the National Assembly to Premier Bourassa are directly opposed to what Canadians and Quebecers want on the question of Senate reform.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, these days just about everyone is an environmentalist and that is a very good development.
It is also important to be an informed environmentalist. A lot of members of parliament, broadcasters, journalists, and others, quite often refer to aerosol sprays as containing CFCs. I know, because a lot of these products are made in Etobicoke-Lakeshore.
Since 1976 industry itself has been phasing out the use of chlorofluorocarbons or CFCs as propellants in aerosol sprays. In fact, only a small number of aerosol sprays, those that are used in prescription pharmaceuticals, which are less than 5 per cent, are still used in Canada.
Within the next two weeks, regulations will be promulgated under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act which will further solve this problem by closing off any remaining imports of aerosol sprays with CFCs.
June 12, 1990

Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands -
Canso): Madam Speaker, Canada has always been recognized around the world as an international peacekeeper. We have the prospect of being a world leader in environmental technology. There is a project before the government that can support both objectives.
Thyssen-Bear Head Industries has proposed to provide our Armed Forces with a modern multi-purpose vehicle for use in peacekeeping and other defence-related activities. In addition, it promises to bring to Canada access to German environmental technology that is state of the art and in use across Europe.
Thyssen-Bear Head Industries, therefore, could be a vehicle by which Canada becomes a world environmental leader. Moreover, Thyssen-Bear Head, along with Scotia Synfuels, offers two of the most promising industrial opportunities for the Strait of Canso area, an area where lasting jobs are urgently needed. We have the facilities: a world-class superport and excellent industrial training centres. Our skilled tradespeople are second to none.
I have spoken before in support of the Thyssen-Bear Head Industries project and the economic benefits it would provide in eastern Nova Scotia. I want to express this support again.
I urge the Canadian government to act soon to enable this project, which has been in abeyance since 1988, to go forward.

Madam Speaker, few Canadians know that between 1914 and 1920 thousands of Ukrainian Canadians and other east Europeans were interned unjustly in 26 camps set up across Canada.
Subsequently tens of thousands more were designated as enemy aliens, disenfranchised, and subjected to various other discriminatory measures legislated by the Government of Canada. The property of many so-called
enemy aliens was confiscated and never returned. This is a shameful episode in our history.
Today I met with the redress committee of the Ukrainian Canadian Congress. The Ukrainian Canadian Congress has joined with Italian, Chinese, and Japanese communities to form the National Redress Alliance.
The New Democratic Party supports the creation of a national redress commission to deal expeditiously and justly with these dark episodes in our history.
I call on the government to establish immediately such a commission to deal with the issues of Ukrainians and other groups which deserve a fair hearing for the injustices of the past.

subtopic: EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
EUROPEAN BANK FOR RECONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to congratulate the government on its decision to participate in the newly formed European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. This bank will assist east bloc countries make the transition from socialist economies to free market economies.
I know that many people across Saskatchewan will welcome this effort to assist their friends and relatives in improving their lives. After 40 years of stagnation and repression it would be almost impossible for these nations to rebuild without help from the west. As well, Canadian participation in the bank will help to enhance the Canadian business access to commercial opportunities in eastern Europe.
I believe that despite our own difficult financial situation it would be short-sighted and inappropriate to ignore the plight of newly reformed democracies in eastern Europe.

Mr. Speaker, the National Institute for International Affairs sponsored a delegation to observe the June 8 and June 9, 1990 Czechoslovakian election, the first truly competitive election since 1946.

June 12, 1990
Oral Questions
I was pleased an invitation was extended to me to join this observer team. The delegation was led by U.S. Senators John McCain of Arizona and Chris Dodd of Connecticut. In addition to business representatives, parliamentarians from Panama, Hungary, Chile, Columbia, Australia, and other nations were present.
The election marked the culmination of a remarkable series of events that have transformed Czechoslovakia during the past seven months. The election demonstrated the vitality of Czechoslovakia's democratic culture and the country rejoining, at least in part, the European community to which it historically belonged.
We should also congratulate Elections Canada for contributing advice in the planning of the Czechoslovakian voting. Its guidance and assistance was noted to me by the Czech election committee.
I was most pleased to be invited to be a witness in this historic event. I saw a country that has now just ran the first yard of a 100-yard dash and, in their own words, Czechs and Slovaks acknowledge they have many hurdles yet to overcome.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister.
In his speech to the House yesterday, referring to his recent closed door marathon sessions with the provincial premiers, the Prime Minister said:
This process has proven to be increasingly unsatisfactory in several respects and must be changed.
There should, first and foremost, be ample opportunity for Canadians to participate in the process.
Yet, in an interview published today in The Globe and Mail referring to these recent seven-day marathon closed sessions he held with the provincial premiers, the Prime Minister said:
That's the way it had to be done. You're asking me if I had any regrets? None whatsoever.
I ask the Prime Minister: How can Canadians take the Prime Minister seriously when one day he says he wants to change the process and the next day he says he has no regrets about it whatsoever?

Because, Mr. Speaker, there is no contradiction whatsoever. In regard to the process that we followed, it was a process that I inherited pursuant to both past practice and events that developed from the 1981-82 constitutional debates and negotiations here in Ottawa.
Yesterday I was speaking of my personal opinion in regard to this process, which personally I find unacceptable and I announced yesterday will be changed presumably by the House of Commons for all constitutional matters in the future.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Constitution as adopted in 1982 does not require the sessions between himself and premiers on constitutional change to be marathon sessions, nor does it require these sessions to be held in secret. Certainly he was not bound by anything in that regard in our Constitution.
In the same interview in The Globe and Mail the Prime Minister, speaking of this meeting with the provincial premiers, said:
I told (my advisers) a month ago when we were going to meet. It's
like an election campaign; you count backward. I said: "that's the
day we are going to roll the dice."
Yet, for weeks the Prime Minister left the impression with Canadians and with this House that he and Senator Murray were engaged in a difficult search for common ground as a prerequisite, as a basis for calling a First Ministers' Conference and not deliberately waiting until the last minute to call a First Ministers' Conference in order to roll the dice with the country possibly at stake.
I ask the Prime Minister: Why did he tell Canadians that he was trying to find consensus among the provinces before calling a First Ministers' Conference when he now admits that all he was doing was waiting until the last minute to roll the dice with the premiers? Is this the way the Prime Minister is really attempting to carry out national reconciliation and build the future of this country?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know why the Leader of the Opposition is so offended. The process produced the signature of 10 premiers promoting the concept of a united Canada. I would have thought he would would celebrate that.
June 12, 1990
Hear, hear.

There is nothing very mysterious or sinister about the statement. When on May 111 met with my advisers the first thing we had to look at was the entire schedule of commitments I had entered into as Prime Minister of Canada from June 23 leading back to May 11.
At that point in time this was the relatively fixed schedule that I faced. The Charest committee would report the end of the following week, and during that week there was a state visit of President Gonzalez of Spain. After the Charest report on May 17, Senator Murray would carry out consultations across the country with each premier. That took three days and had to be done before any calling of a conference.
My friend will remember that a House order had already been passed in regard to Bill C-43. Along with most members of the House I was here until late the night of May 23 with the report stage votes.
I began extensive meetings with each premier a day and a half later. They took place over four days from May 25 to May 28. These meetings were obviously necessary before convoking a full conference.
On the day of the last meeting, May 28, there was an official state visit to Ottawa by the Secretary General of the United Nations, and I had undertaken on behalf of all Canadians to speak at a state dinner in his honour in Toronto that night.
On the next day President Gorbachev of the Soviet Union arrived for May 29 and May 30.
Time, time.

That left three days before the First Ministers' Conference. My hon. friend should be congratulating the Prime Minister of Canada for doing all that with his colleagues, representing Canada, and trying to bring Canada together with the support of all members of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister did not give any of those explanations to the Globe and Mail. Why, in his interview with the Globe and Mail, did he only mention how he planned the process like an election campaign? There
Oral Questions
was no reference to the Prime Minister of Spain. Even though he said in the interview that he had no regrets about the methods used, will he give us a commitment today that he will seriously try to change a process everyone now says must be changed?

Mr. Speaker, of course I do not for a moment question what was reported by the Globe and Mail journalists. Certainly not! I said yesterday in the House that it was an outdated procedure that obviously needed to be changed. I announced yesterday that we intend to change the procedure to provide for more active participation by all Canadians before a new constitutional amendment is ratified.
The hon. member talked about methods. In 1981-82, we had a Constitution with nine provinces out of ten. I managed to get ten out of ten.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the House was advised that shortly after Route Canada failed there were charges laid under the Canada Labour Act.
We are not dealing here with employer-employee relations. We are dealing with over $21 million of taxpayers' and employees' trust money that was spent out of trust. Mr. Speaker, when money is spent out of trust by a company like Route Canada or Route Canada Enterprises, you can pierce a corporate veil and look to the directors of the company for reimbursement of those trust funds.
I ask the Minister of Transport to pierce the corporate veil and make sure that the directors of that corporation, including the Fingolds, reimburse the employees of Route Canada and the taxpayers of this country in excess of $21 million.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my hon. friend's comments about the corporate veil and trust. My hon. friend will know that the company holds those funds in trust for the various government departments and is required to remit those to the department.

June 12, 1990
Oral Questions
Once a company goes into bankruptcy, all the assets are seized by the receiver in bankruptcy who takes charge of the assets, calculates the liabilities, and pays the appropriate liabilities, whether they are secured or preferred, out of the funds that he or she receives.
I expect the Registrar in Bankruptcy will take care of that matter in due course.

Mr. Speaker, I guess the essence of the question to the same minister is: if there is a shortfall, does the minister intend to go after the directors of that company to make up the shortfall in the trust funds that were spent out of trust by the directors of Route Canada and Route Enterprises Canada Limited?
I think what this situation needs is a full, open and complete investigation into all the affairs as they affect the disposition of Route Canada by CN and CN Rail. I ask the minister to commence a complete, open investigation into this aborted transaction.

Mr. Speaker, to the best of my knowledge the bankruptcy proceedings have not been wound up. I would think that in the normal course of events the Registrar in Bankruptcy will report as to whether or not there have been any illegalities.
All the creditors will be paid in accordance with their preference, preferred or secured. I do not think it would be appropriate to step in with a full investigation until the bankruptcy proceedings are completed.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. About a month ago, the Charest Report was published. The committee had heard 160 witnesses and received 800 briefs and papers. It was an exercise in public consultation. Now we hear that the Prime Minister already had the whole thing planned, even before the committee started its work. It would seem the Charest Report has now become the "charade" report.
I have the following question for the Prime Minister: Is the Prime Minister saying that the committee's work was just a facade to hide the government's real agenda?

Mr. Speaker, I have already had occasion to praise the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, from Saskatchewan, who was an active participant in the committee, so I think it is clear I was very serious about its proceedings.
I said earlier to the Leader of the Opposition that the explanation was quite simple. The Charest Report was released on May 17, before a long weekend. We had three weeks left. During the first week, we had Senator Murray's visits and my meetings with the Premiers. During the second week, which started on May 27,1 had an official visit by Perez de Cuellar and the official visit of President Gorbachev, and in the third week we started the process of meeting with the Premiers on June 3. So there is nothing out of the ordinary in all this.
It was simply a matter of looking at our agenda for the period from May 11 to June 23 and deciding when we could send Senator Murray on his mission, when I could meet the provincial Premiers, individually and together, at my residence, and when I could fulfil my international obligations on behalf of Canada, with the meetings with President Gorbachev, the Secretary General of the U.N. and the president of Spain. I did all that, and then I held our meeting.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, obviously the Prime Minister cannot answer the question. The members of this party participated in the Charest committee in good faith. The public participated in the Charest committee in good faith. Yet this government has not shown good faith with the public of Canada.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister about the process that happened over this past week. We know that late Thursday night the Prime Minister's office met with Jean Chretien's national chairman, his policy adviser and one of his lawyers, while aboriginal people and women stood on the outside.
June 12, 1990

Even though the future of aboriginal people and women was at stake, can the Prime Minister explain why meeting with Mr. Chretien's campaign officials was so central to his plan?

Mr. Speaker, there are many things that I have in mind for Mr. Chretien but that is not one of them.
I think my hon. friend should know that I spent the time before the meeting of the First Ministers meeting, as well on the Sunday, with the leaders of the territorial governments, Yukon and the Northwest Territories, both of whom had an agenda very largely committed to the concerns that my hon. friend has just raised.
I trust that my hon. friend will not blame me for failing to meet with anyone other than First Ministers and territorial leaders. I sought to meet with many more but there are only so many hours in a day.
I think that my hon. friend, had she the time to listen to the speeches made by the territorial leaders late Saturday night at the Conference Centre, would agree that they seemed to indicate generally that they were very pleased with the way the matter had been conducted and that they were very pleased with the results, and hoped for even better results in the future.

Mr. Speaker, aboriginal people were on the outside of this process. Women were on the outside of this process. Yes, the Prime Minister's office met with the elected premier of the Yukon, the elected government leader of the Northwest Territories.
Will the Prime Minister explain to this House what the role of Mr. Chretien's advisers was in his plan which he said was necessary to bring forward the constitutional talks of last week?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: He's the next Prime Minister, your successor.

Mr. Speaker, I was asked by the Liberals to say it is because he is the next Prime Minister. They also asked me to say that about the last leader of the Liberal party, and I do not want to damage Mr. Chretien before he starts.
My hon. friend raises some very good questions. With regard to the issues that are raised, I think she would be
Oral Questions
pleased to note that in the final document that was published there is great care in the matter of gender equality, which was a matter of concern to the Leader of the NDP in Manitoba for example. There are provisions to ensure a fundamental new process-
Are those Mr. Chretien's provisions, or what?
Mr. Speaker, I am trying to answer the Leader of the NDP on a very important matter.
Answer the question.

We put in place a brand new series of provisions for a constitutional process for aboriginal Canadians.
The Northwest Territories were ensured of a priority analysis of their provincehood requirements, not based on 1982 but going back to Confederation, namely, provincehood on the basis of an agreement between the federal government and the territories themselves.
There was further consideration in respect of appointments of senators and justices of the Supreme Court from the territories. There was very ample consideration given to the concerns of the north as reflected by the statements of the two territorial leaders.
If my hon. friend is blaming some member of my staff or anyone else for listening to constructive ideas from members of the Liberal Party or the NDP, then I do not think that that would be appropriate. I listened to and received very many constructive ideas and helpful suggestions from the NDP and from all kinds of Liberals. I acknowledged that publicly yesterday.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish to draw to members' attention the presence in the gallery of Volodymyr Yavorivsky, National Deputy to the Supreme Soviet of the U.S.S.R. and Ukraine and Vice President of Rukh.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I also wish to draw to members' attention the presence in the gallery of Volodymyr Mokry, Deputy to the Polish Parliament.

Hear, hear!

June 12, 1990
Oral Questions TRADE

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister.
While the Prime Minister has been preoccupied with constitutional matters, I am sure he is aware of the important decision taken by the Presidents of the United States and Mexico to begin talks leading toward what the U.S. President calls a North American trade agreement. I think he also recognizes that it is equally important that Canadians understand what this government intends to do about it.
In those circumstances I would like to ask the Prime Minister to confirm that the cabinet has already met on this very important item and has decided not to become involved in negotiations. Will he confirm that that decision has been made? Will he tell us what in fact the cabinet has authorized government officials to do to respond to this veiy crucial initiative that will affect Canada in a dramatic way?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the cabinet has made no decision as to whether we wish to be further involved in this matter or not further involved in this matter because the matter has hardly even commenced as yet.
There has been a decision between the U.S. and Mexico that they wish to have preliminary discussions and consultations to see whether or not they wish to engage in negotiations with reference to a free trade agreement.

speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen- Merritt had just completed his speech. We will now proceed with questions and comments following that speech. The hon. member for Sudbury.

Madam Speaker, I listened very carefully to my colleague's speech and I must say that I do agree with many of his comments. Bill C-52 is certainly not a perfect piece of legislation. The complexity of the pension reform has made it very difficult for us to judge absolutely every aspect and to make sure that everything is as equitable as it should be.
As a result of that, we have insisted that there be a full and complete review of the legislation and of the pension system after three years of implementation of Bill C-52. We certainly hope that any problems that have come up during that time could be addressed, if not even prior to the three years.
On the other hand, my hon. colleague mentioned that his party believes that we should have a beefed-up Canada Pension Plan. I would like to remind the hon. member that we have also requested that a review of the
Government Orders
Canada Pension Plan be done by the finance committee within the next year. I personally feel that there is a place for Canada Pension Plan but that there is also a place for Registered Retirement Savings Plans and that both can exist together and complement each other.
I do not know if the hon. member would like to comment on these two aspects of Bill C-52.

Madam Speaker, to take the last part of the comments of my colleague from Sudbury first, I do not disagree at all that the two programs can co-exist. In fact, I think they have done fairly well. What I am afraid of is a continuation of what I see as the thread of what has been happening since 1984 with the privatization of a number of programs. I fear that with the raising of the limits of the Registered Retirement Savings Plan and dropping the percentage of earned wages from 20 to 18 per cent, we are moving closer and closer to privatization of pension plans.
If the review is done with the idea of ensuring that all Canadians will ultimately benefit through an expansion of the Canada Pension Plan, Old Age Security, or the Guaranteed Income Supplement, that is fair enough. But what I fear is that the program as set out in Bill C-52 will ultimately erode the system that we have and we will depend more and more on privatization. In other words, people will be encouraged to invest in private pensions plans as opposed to plans such as the Canada Pension Plan which people like Mr. Knowles and Tommy Douglas have fought for in the past.
The review process, in the absence of any real amendments, is an excellent idea as long as it takes into consideration all Canadians from all walks of life rather than, as we have seen in the past with the goods and services tax and the Unemployment Insurance Commission, a very limited number of people being able to give their ideas and impressions on the Registered Retirement Savings Plan. I want to have a system where people can actually be listened to and heard. I do not want a system under which we set deadlines and then leave out most of the people who want to speak as we did on the goods and services tax. On that legislation we heard less than 300 of well over 1,000 representations that requested to be heard.
So let us listen to all suggestions and use some of those suggestions in order to make the Canada Pension Plan system better for all of us.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words regarding Bill C-52, an act to amend the Income Tax Act relating to RRSPs. While I had intended to speak at some length I do not believe that is necessary. The member for Essex-Windsor and his colleague from Kootenay East worked very diligently in the committee examining Bill C-52. I want to commend them for the job they did in that committee. While there are still many problems associated with this legislation regarding RRSPs, as a result of their work and that of others in opposition it is tremendously improved. On behalf of us all I want to recognize the efforts that the opposition made in improving this legislation.
I also listened carefully to my hon. colleague and friend from Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt. Ele largely laid out the concerns the New Democratic Party has with the general thrust of this legislation.
The legislation starts, in my judgment, at the wrong point. It aims to allow everyone earning up to $86,000 a year to shelter from taxes the same percentage of income. Obviously that is going to benefit those in the upper income brackets.
On principle we have to ask ourselves whether it is the role of legislation to identity those who are the wealthiest and in relatively privileged positions in our society and arrange legislation such that they benefit much more than people from a low income bracket.
I believe that not only is that the wrong starting point, it also means that tax sheltering of our income becomes the major thrust of most pension-related savings as opposed to the approach which expands the Canada Pension Plan in order to provide satisfactory pension levels for everyone in the Canadian workforce.
Stanley Knowles and many others dedicated their entire lives to improving the Canada Pension Plan. Today, as opposed to improving the Canada Pension Plan so that all Canadians can benefit, we are tinkering around with tax legislation that enables certain people to avoid tax as they set aside money for their retirement years. We are seeing a departure from a trend over the years to improve the Canada Pension Plan. Now we are seeing a trend toward the privatization of our pension system.
It is important to recognize that only 20 per cent of all tax filers take advantage of RRSPs. Five per cent of Canadians earning under $15,000 contribute to RRSPs whereas nearly 60 per cent of Canadians earning over $50,000 contribute to RRSPs. We see with a glance at these simple statistics that the RRSP legislation is earmarked for those who are in the upper income brackets of our society.
The work of the committee has brought about positive changes including improvements to pension affordability, the provisions to allow for earlier retirement, changes in definition of designated plans and respect for existing contribution levels under collective agreements. I want to acknowledge and recognize these and other improvements, as well as saying that I and my colleagues depart from the major thrust of the legislation which is essentially pension reform through tax alteration, which is not the approach that we feel is most appropriate.
I would remiss if I did not note from the comments of previous speakers and the work of my colleagues on the committee the continuing complexity associated with this legislation. I read with interest the evidence of the professional actuaries who spoke to the committee and suggested that the incredible complexity of this legislation will make it essentially unworkable. In the minds of these experts, the legislation cannot work, it is simply too complex.
As a result of the efforts of my colleagues in opposition, a three-year review period has been introduced so that at least every three years we can revisit the changed legislation to see if in fact it is working and serving the purposes for which it was intended, even though we might question those purposes.
It has been suggested that these changes in Bill C-52 will cost employers an estimated $60 to $70 million in start-up costs and an annual reporting cost of between $10 and $15 million. With high interest rates, with the goods and services tax coming, with the changes to the unemployment insurance legislation that will expect more of employers, and now with Bill C-52, how much can a government abuse the small and medium sized business sector? There is a limit, and I suspect that we have nearly reached it now.
In conclusion, while we recognize that improvements have occurred in this legislation as a result of the excellent committee work and an acknowledgement by the government that changes to this legislation were desired, we will oppose the legislation on the grounds of

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with pleasure that I introduce and present this Private Member's Bill S-16 to the House today. The bill is based on a petition that was presented to Parliament by the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy to enact a name change for the institute to the Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum.
The institute, which has its head office in Montreal, is a non-profit corporation that has been in existence since before the turn of the century. In fact, it is very interesting to all my colleagues to note that the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy was incorporated by Parliament under Chapter 96 of the Statutes of Canada in 1898.
The objectives of the institute are to promote the arts and sciences connected with the economical production of valuable minerals and metals by means of meetings for the reading and discussion of technical papers and the establishment of a central reference library; to take concerted action upon matters as affect the mining and metallurgical industries in Canada; and, of course, to encourage and promote these industries by lawful and honourable means.
The institute publishes a number of journals in which the most worthy of its technical papers are featured. These journals provide a forum for the exchange of technical information among approximately 11,000 people who are currently members of the institute.
In any given year, 10 to 15 technical meetings are organized and held in various parts of Canada. These meetings are attended by some 6,000 to 7,000 delegates who participate in as many as 1,300 technical information sessions that are held each and every year.
The members are grouped into eight technical divisions according to their professional disciplines and field of interest-coal, geology, industrial minerals, metallurgy, mineral processing, metal mining, maintenance engineering, and petroleum. There is also a geographical

June 12, 1990
Private Members' Business
grouping made up of six districts integrating the 65 branches located in most cities with a mining or a petroleum background.
The petroleum society of the institute has been assuming a greater role of importance in the affairs of this organization for many years. It has about 2,500 members in its ranks and represents the fastest growing division within the institute.
A task force was appointed in December 1987 to study the consideration of a name change to include petroleum, and this change was proposed to the general membership which overwhelmingly favoured it. So the wheels were set in motion to petition Parliament to pass a bill to change the name of the institute to the Canadian Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Petroleum, which truly reflects the interests of its membership.
This change of name is one of the purposes of Bill S-16 before us today. As you can see, Madam Speaker, the bill was passed through the Senate on June 5, 1990.
The bill also contains a few technical and incidental changes to the corporation's charter. One amendment would clarify the corporate powers and management of the institute and at the same time remove a restriction on the total value of real estate that may be held at any one time by the institute.
Another amendment is designed to provide the institute with general borrowing powers which it does not have today and which of course can restrict the operation. This establishment does not rely on government funding and therefore these particular changes are at no cost to the Government of Canada.
Madam Speaker, Bill S-16 is straight forward. I have reviewed the amendments with you and with my colleagues here in the House today. I would very much like it to go through all stages today so that we can report it back as carried.

Madam Speaker, at this moment it would be my intention to seek unanimous consent of the House to suspend the sitting, for a few minutes, to the call of the Chair, which we would anticipate being about four o'clock, for the purpose of Royal Assent.
June 12, 1990

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The House has heard the suggestion made by the hon. member. Is there unanimous consent?

Agreed.
The sitting of the House was suspended at 3.29 p.m.
The House resumed at 4.49 p.m.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have the honour to inform the House that a message has been received from the Senate informing this House that the Senate has passed Bill C-65, an Act to provide borrowing authority, without amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that a communication has been received as follows:
Rideau Hall Ottawa,
June 12, 1990 Sir,
I have the honour to inform you that the Honourable John Sopinka, Puisne Judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, in his capacity as Deputy Governor General, will proceed to the Senate Chamber today, the 12th day of June, at 4:30 p.m., for the purpose of giving Royal Assent to certain Bills.
Yours sincerely,
Leopold H. Amyot Secretary to the Governor General

A message was delivered by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod as follows:
Royal Assent
Madam Speaker, the Honourable Deputy to the Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable House in the Chamber of the honourable th Senate.
Accordingly, Madam Speaker with the House went up to the Senate chamber.
And being returned:
['Agreed.\nThe sitting of the House was suspended at 5.02 p.m.']

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that when the House went up to the Senate Chamber the Deputy Governor General was pleased to give, in Her Majesty's name, the Royal Assent to the following Bill:
Bill C-25, an Act to amend the Geneva Conventions Act, the National Defence Act and the Trade-marks Act- Chapter 14.
Bill C-53, An Act to amend the Criminal Code (arson)- Chapter
Bill C-59, an Act to amend various Acts to give effect to the reconstitution of the courts in British Columbia-Chapter 16.
Bill C-60, an Act to amend various Acts to give effect to the reconstitution of the courts in Ontario and to provide for other related matters-Chapter 17.
Bill C-61, An Act to amend the Divorce Act (barriers to religious remarriage)-Chapter 18.
Bill C-65, an Act to provide borrowing authority-Chapter 19.
Bill S-10, an Act respecting the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants.
Bill S-15, an Act to amend the Act of incorporation of Desjardins Mutual Life Assurance Company.
Madam Speaker, on a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Ka-mouraska-Riviere-du-Loup, on a point of order.
Madam Speaker, I believe we have unanimous consent to suspend the proceedings of the House until the vote at 6 p.m.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The House has heard the suggestion of the hon. member. Is there unanimous consent to suspend the sitting until 6 p.m.?

Agreed.
The sitting of the House was suspended at 5.02 p.m.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 6 p.m.
Government Orders

The House resumed from Monday, June 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-69, an Act to amend certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures, be read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It being six o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 45(5)(a), the House will now proceed to the deferred division on the motion of the Minister of Finance for third reading of Bill C-69, an Act to amend certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures.
Call in the members.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I declare the motion carried.	
Bill read the third time and passed.
June 12, 1990
Madam Speaker, unfortunately I was delayed at a meeting. Had I been here, I would have voted with my party on this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think perhaps you might find unanimous agreement if we were to call it ten o'clock and proceed with the late show.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that there is unanimous consent to call it ten o'clock?

Agreed.
Adjournment Debate
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 38 deemed to have been moved.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I see that none of the members who had requested to participate in this motion are now present.
Accordingly, the motion to adjourn the House is now deemed to have been adopted. This House stands adjourned until tomorrow at 2 p.m., pursuant to Standing Order 24(1).
The House adjourned at 6.32 p.m.
Wednesday, June 13, 1990
